data.title: Keratosis pilaris — viva
data.summary: Disorders of keratinisation · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Keratosis pilaris** (Disorders of keratinisation)_

**Q1. What is keratosis pilaris (KP)?**
- Very common, benign, inherited (autosomal dominant with variable penetrance) follicular keratinisation disorder: rough, skin-coloured to red, keratotic follicular papules ('chicken skin') on extensor upper arms, thighs, buttocks, cheeks (children)
- Begins in childhood, peaks in adolescence, improves with age; worse in winter/dry climate

**Q2. Associations.**
- Atopic dermatitis and ichthyosis vulgaris (FLG mutations), obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, Down syndrome, Noonan/cardiofaciocutaneous syndromes, drugs (BRAF inhibitors — vemurafenib, lithium)

**Q3. Variants.**
- KP rubra (prominent erythema), KP alba
- Keratosis pilaris atrophicans group: ulerythema ophryogenes (lateral eyebrows — atrophy and loss; Noonan, Cornelia de Lange), atrophoderma vermiculatum (honeycomb atrophy on cheeks), keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans (X-linked, scarring alopecia of scalp, photophobia)
- Erythromelanosis follicularis faciei et colli (red-brown pigmentation with follicular papules on cheeks/neck)
- Keratosis pilaris rubra faceii

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Keratin plug distending the follicular infundibulum, often with a coiled/twisted hair, mild perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Phrynoderma (nutritional; elbows/knees, larger spiny papules), lichen spinulosus (grouped spiny papules), Darier's disease (greasy seborrhoeic distribution), PRP (follicular knuckle papules), folliculitis (pustules), lichen nitidus, scurvy (perifollicular haemorrhages, corkscrew hairs), follicular eczema, acne (comedones)

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Reassurance — benign, improves with age
- Emollients and keratolytics: urea 10–20%, lactic acid 12%, salicylic acid 3–6%, glycolic acid; gentle exfoliation
- Topical retinoids (tretinoin, adapalene, tazarotene); short course of mild topical steroids for red/itchy KP
- Lasers: PDL/KTP for erythema, long-pulsed Nd:YAG/diode laser hair removal, Q-switched Nd:YAG for pigmentation; microdermabrasion

**Q7. Describe the process of keratinisation and the cornified envelope (PYQ).**
- Basal keratinocytes (K5/K14) divide and move up: spinous (K1/K10, desmosomes), granular (keratohyaline granules — profilaggrin, loricrin; lamellar bodies — lipids), cornified layer (flattened anucleate corneocytes)
- Cornified envelope: cross-linked proteins (involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich proteins) by transglutaminases (TGM1, TGM3, TGM5) with covalently bound lipid envelope (ceramides); intercellular lipid lamellae (ceramides, cholesterol, FFA) — 'bricks and mortar' barrier
- Desquamation via kallikreins (KLK5/7) degrading corneodesmosomes, regulated by LEKTI (SPINK5)

**Q8. Describe the clinical features in detail.**
- Small (1–2 mm) rough follicular keratotic papules ('chicken skin'/ 'goose bumps'), sometimes with perifollicular erythema, on extensor upper arms, thighs, buttocks, cheeks (children); asymptomatic or mildly itchy; worse in winter; improves after adolescence

**Q9. Treatment in detail.**
- Emollients with keratolytics — urea 10–20%, lactic acid 12%, salicylic acid 2–6%, glycolic acid; topical retinoids (tretinoin, adapalene), mild steroids for inflamed lesions; gentle exfoliation; pulsed-dye laser/ Nd:YAG/ IPL for erythema; microdermabrasion; recurrence on stopping

**Q10. What drugs cause KP-like eruptions?**
- BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib, dabrafenib), nilotinib, sorafenib, ciclosporin (also trichodysplasia spinulosa)

**Q11. Ulerythema ophryogenes and Noonan syndrome link.**
- Lateral eyebrow erythema with follicular papules → scarring loss of eyebrows; associated with Noonan syndrome, cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome, Cornelia de Lange, Rubinstein–Taybi, woolly hair — examine for dysmorphism

**Q12. Differentiate KP from phrynoderma.**
- KP: atopic/ genetic, upper outer arms/ thighs, fine papules, normal nutrition; phrynoderma: larger spiny papules on elbows/ knees/ buttocks, malnutrition signs (night blindness, Bitot's spots, angular cheilitis), responds to vitamin/ nutritional supplementation

**Q13. What is the pathogenesis?**
- Abnormal follicular keratinisation with keratin plug in the infundibulum, often encircling a coiled hair; associated with filaggrin mutations (ichthyosis vulgaris, atopy); worse in winter (low humidity), improves in summer and with age

**Q14. Describe keratosis pilaris atrophicans variants.**
- Ulerythema ophryogenes (lateral eyebrows — erythema, papules, loss of eyebrows; Noonan syndrome, Cornelia de Lange), atrophoderma vermiculatum (honeycomb pitting of cheeks), keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans (X-linked — scarring alopecia, photophobia)

**Q15. What is keratosis pilaris rubra?**
- Variant with prominent erythema extending beyond the follicular papules (face, arms) — pulsed-dye laser helps erythema

## Quick spotter facts
- Rough follicular papules on outer arms of an atopic adolescent — keratosis pilaris
- Ulerythema ophryogenes — lateral eyebrow loss

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Follicular keratoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
